questions.q: What real format does each audience's final presentation actually take?
options: A single generic PDF summary adapted for all three audiences
All three audiences receive only the Excel workbook
Executives get a live Power BI session, the Board gets the published Tableau Public deck, and Finance gets the reconciled Excel workbook itself
Executives and the Board both get the same Tableau deck
questions.explain: Each audience receives the real, finished version of the exact deliverable Lesson 1 originally scoped for them — three independently real artifacts, not one summary reshaped three ways.

questions.q: How does the level of detail about Chapter 7's discrepancy differ between Finance and the Executives/Board?
options: Finance gets the full, specific story (the bug, how it was found, the fix); Executives and the Board get an honest but shorter summary that a discrepancy was found and corrected before the meeting
Finance is told nothing, since they already know; Executives and the Board get the full technical breakdown
The discrepancy is never disclosed to anyone outside the data team
All three audiences receive the identical level of technical detail
questions.explain: Both versions are honest and accurate — the difference is which level of detail actually serves each audience, not whether anything is hidden.

questions.q: Why is hiding the already-fixed discrepancy from every audience the wrong instinct, according to this lesson?
options: Because an honest, audience-appropriate disclosure is both possible and preferable to hiding a mistake that's already fixed — the two are not the same thing
Because Finance would discover the omission and refuse to sign off regardless
Because it's illegal to withhold any spreadsheet error from a board
Because Power BI automatically logs every change for auditors to see
questions.explain: The lesson draws a distinction between full transparency (which is achievable at the right level of detail for each audience) and burying a non-technical audience in syntax they don't need.

questions.q: What did this capstone's shared-warehouse architecture actually accomplish this quarter, concretely?
options: It made the Tableau deck load faster than it otherwise would have
It allowed Finance to skip building their own workbook
It eliminated the need for Chapter 3's Python validation entirely
It caught a real, specific error in Finance's Excel formula and got it corrected before it ever reached a board meeting
questions.explain: Having three independently-built totals is exactly what surfaced and let the team fix the quarter-boundary bug before the Board ever saw an incorrect number.

questions.q: What would have happened if Finance's Excel workbook had been the ONLY deliverable this quarter, with no independent Power BI or Tableau totals to check it against?
options: The bug would have been caught immediately by Excel's own error checking
The double-counting error would likely have gone to the Board uncaught, since nothing independent existed to reveal the mismatch
The warehouse would have automatically corrected the formula
Nothing would be different, since Excel formulas are always self-validating
questions.explain: Without an independently-built second or third total to compare against, there would have been no way to notice the small, repeatable discrepancy before it reached the Board.
